analysis.one_liner: Rolls back the 2001 tax cuts for top earners and large estates to protect Social Security, Medicare, schools, and housing.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003, leaving the 2001 tax cuts in place.
analysis.plain_summary: Two months after the September 11 attacks, Representative Jan Schakowsky proposed slowing down the 2001 tax cuts (the Bush tax cuts) until Congress had met five public priorities: relief for 9/11 victims, protecting Social Security and Medicare, a Medicare prescription drug benefit, federal money to modernize schools and hire 100,000 teachers, and reducing severe housing needs. The bill would have raised the top income tax rates back toward pre-cut levels, kept the estate tax instead of letting it be repealed, and exempted family-owned businesses from estate tax up to $4 million. It was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules committees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary people would have benefited indirectly: the 2001 tax cuts' high-income provisions would have been scaled back, preserving federal revenue, and the bill created a standing task force to certify whether Congress had delivered 9/11 victim relief, protected the Social Security and Medicare trust funds, enacted a Medicare drug benefit, funded school repairs and 100,000 new teachers, and reduced worst-case housing needs [S2][S3]. Family-owned businesses would have gained a much larger estate tax deduction, $4 million instead of $675,000 [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working families, Medicare beneficiaries, and family businesses

how_it_helps.text: Restores the top income tax rates toward their pre-2001 levels, reaching 39.6% by 2002, while leaving middle and lower rates largely intact, preserving federal revenue [S3].

Repeals the scheduled repeal of the estate tax, so large estates remain taxed at death, and retains the phaseout of personal exemptions and limitations on itemized deductions for high earners [S2][S3].
Raises the estate tax deduction for family-owned business interests from $675,000 to $4,000,000, shielding family businesses from the estate tax the bill keeps in place [S3].

Creates a National Priorities Assessment Task Force of senior House and Senate committee leaders that must certify five goals before reporting: 9/11 victim relief, Social Security and Medicare trust fund security, a comprehensive Medicare prescription drug benefit, federal funding for school modernization and hiring 100,000 teachers, and a significant reduction in worst-case housing needs [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households in the top income tax brackets would have paid higher rates (39.6% restored by 2002, plus reinstated limits on deductions and exemptions), and heirs of the largest estates would have continued to owe estate tax that the 2001 law had scheduled to phase out [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The higher top rates would have applied retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2000, raising taxes on top earners during a period when the economy was already weakening [S3].

The task force mechanism ties tax cuts to goals that are not fully within Congress's control (such as reducing worst-case housing needs), which critics would call an imprecise trigger for tax policy [S3].
Keeping the estate tax while carving out a $4 million deduction for family-owned businesses would invite valuation disputes over what counts as a family business interest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded tax cuts concentrated on the highest earners and largest estates for protection of federal revenue and a public scorecard on priorities like a Medicare drug benefit and school funding. The cost fell entirely on high-income households and large estates, though raising taxes retroactively into an economic downturn was a real objection, and the task force trigger was blunt. On the merits it was a straightforward redistribution question: modestly more revenue and public priorities versus lower taxes at the top.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules committees the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Representative Jan Schakowsky introduced the First Things First Act on October 2, 2001, with 14 original cosponsors including Representatives Barbara Lee, Bernie Sanders, Dennis Kucinich, and Henry Waxman [S3].

The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means and additionally to the Committee on Rules, a dual referral that gives each committee control only over the provisions in its jurisdiction [S1][S5].
No committee action, hearing, or vote followed; the complete action history shows only the introduction and the referral [S5].
The bill gathered 16 cosponsors — 15 House Democrats and 1 Independent — and none from the Republican majority that controlled the committee agenda [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill expired in committee [S1].
Because the bill never advanced, the 2001 tax law's phased-in rate cuts and its scheduled phaseout of the estate tax remained on the books as written [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households and heirs of large estates were better off, because the 2001 tax cuts' top-rate reductions, deduction and exemption provisions, and estate tax phaseout all stayed in force. Congressional Republicans were also better off in that no vote was ever recorded on rolling back the tax cuts.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 2, 2001, framing it as delaying high-income tax cuts until public priorities were met

for.name: 15 of 208 House Democrats and the House's 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 16 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent, with no Republican support

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and never took it up, and no hearing, markup, or vote occurred

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No member of the majority supported the bill, and the chamber never considered it

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, no vote was ever held, and the Republican majority's committees simply never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have restored the 39.6% top rate by 2002 and reinstated the phaseout of personal exemptions and limits on itemized deductions, reversing tax cuts these households had received under the 2001 law [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates and estate planning services
industries.note: The bill repeals the 2001 law's scheduled elimination of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes, so large estates would continue to owe tax and estate planning around the phaseout would keep its role [S2][S3].
The bill raises the estate tax deduction for family-owned business interests from $675,000 to $4 million, substantially shielding family businesses from the estate tax it keeps in place [S3].
